title: Why High-Expectations Charters Fail and How to Hold the Line
author: Educated and Free
summary: A veteran classical-charter-school teacher, writing under the pseudonymous newsletter Educated and Free, dissects why public classical charter schools drift from their founding mission of forming students toward truth, goodness, and beauty. Drawing on two case studies from schools where he taught, he traces a recurring pattern: teachers hired from the conventional public-school pipeline import old habits and shortcuts, parent complaints about rigor pressure administrators to lower standards, and legal exposure from IEP/504 accommodation disputes pushes schools toward blanket grade inflation and diminished expectations for all students. He invokes David Hicks, author of the classical-education treatise Norms and Nobility, who in 2017 concluded classical education was no longer possible even in elite private schools, to argue the challenge is structurally even harder inside public charters funded and regulated by the same state apparatus that runs conventional schools. The piece closes optimistically, framing high-expectations charters as achievable when boards stay mission-aligned and offering readers a free downloadable "Playbook" of systems and policies drawn from his own experience protecting a school's mission from these pressures.
points: Identifies the Charter Board's commitment to Mission, and its management of the single employee it directly controls (the headmaster), as the crucial variable determining whether a classical charter holds its standards or drifts.

Traces two case studies showing how mission drift compounds: teachers import public-school habits under workload pressure, parent complaints push administrators to lower standards, and IEP/504 legal exposure drives blanket grade inflation.

Cites David Hicks, author of the classical-education treatise Norms and Nobility, who despite an elite academic pedigree concluded in 2017 that classical education was 'no longer possible,' to argue public charters face even steeper structural headwinds.

Offers a free downloadable 'Playbook' of editable systems, policies, and accountability tools drawn from real charter experience, intended to help school leaders protect their mission from the pressures described.
quotes: The mission of the typical American classical school is to teach students to love what is True, do what is Good, and defend what is Beautiful. I've watched schools full of students grow toward those things en masse. I've also watched promising schools turn away from their Mission.
The crucial variable in how the school will operate is the Charter Board's understanding of and commitment to the Mission, as well as how they manage their single employee: the Headmaster.
All charter school leaders face a sobering reality: the barbarians don't have to storm the gates. They are already inside.
David Hicks saw this coming. But in 2017, Hicks published an article titled, Is Classical Education Still Possible Today? He answered his own question with a resounding, No.

High Expectations charters can work well when leadership stays mission-aligned, teachers are chosen carefully, and clear systems are in place to maintain standards. The classical tradition is not fragile, having endured far darker times than ours.
